newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel to focus on security in talks with Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Israel to focus on security in talks with Jordan.

text.p: Israeli demands for a Palestinian Authority crackdown on terrorism were set to dominate high-level talks with Jordan on Wednesday.

King Hussein's brother Crown Prince Hassan and Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali were due to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a week after two Arab suicide bombers killed 13 people, and themselves, in a Jerusalem market.
The Jordanian mission to Jerusalem follows efforts by Egypt, Israel's first Arab peace partner, to lower tensions in the region in the aftermath of the attack.

"In (Wednesday's) discussions, there will be no talk...about advancing the peace process until Israel is convinced the Palestinian Authority has begun to fulfil its commitments to fight terrorism," said Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh.

"The whole intention here is to hold serious deliberations with Crown Prince Hassan and the (Jordanian) prime minister on the steps needed to improve the security situation," he told Army Radio on Tuesday.
Naveh said Jordan, which signed a peace treaty with the Jewish state in 1994, had a "joint interest with Israel to wield influence on the Palestinian Authority" to move against Moslem militants.

Netanyahu plans to travel to Jordan next week for talks with King Hussein. Netanyahu's office originally announced the monarch would meet the prime minister in Jerusalem on Wednesday but later said the plans had been revised.

Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak said after meeting Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy in Cairo on Tuesday that Israel should continue talks with the Palestinians because peace was the only way to avoid further terrorism.

The Egyptian leader, responding to Israel's calls for Yasser Arafat to act against anti-Israeli miltants believed to be behind the double bombing, warned of the danger of weakening the Palestinian president's position.
He said Arafat was not "powerful enough" to implement the tough measures Israel demanded of him.
While the security stalemate continued, the military wing of the Islamic militant group Hamas pledged more suicide attacks.
"A chain of martyrdom attacks will come at the appropriate time to hit deep into Zionism," the Izz el-Deen al-Qassam Brigades said in a statement faxed to Reuters in Jerusalem.

The fundamentalist Moslem Shi'ite group Hizbollah, which on Tuesday buried five guerrillas killed by Israeli commandos in south Lebanon, threatened "explosions and suicide bombings" inside "Palestine and...occupied land".
In Amman on Tuesday, Arafat urged the world to act to save the peace process, saying it was endangered by Netanyahu's punitive actions.
Israel closed the West Bank and Gaza after the twin bombing, stopping tens of thousands of Arab workers from reaching their jobs in Israel, paralysing trade and shutting down factories.
Palestinians have said the Israeli measures are collective punishments that weaken Arafat and strengthen extremist forces.

Arafat also attacked Netanyahu personally, saying the Israeli leader was still a political novice. He warned him of the consequences of his treatment of Palestinians, whom he described as a "people who will not be forced to their knees".

Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak issued a statement that the "personal attack on Netanyahu proved Arafat understands that the prime minister's strong policies enjoy the massive support of the overwhelming majority of the Israeli public".
The State Department said on Tuesday Israel's decision to withhold $70 million worth of funds owed to the Palestinian Authority was counter-productive.
"It would be helpful if it was rescinded," State Department spokesman James Foley said.

Israel's Treasury said on Monday it had frozen the transfer of $70 million in VAT and customs duties, which it owes the Palestinian Authority under a 1994 economic protocol, until the Authority stepped up its war against anti-Israel violence.

Foley said U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright planned to travel to the Middle East soon, but not until special U.S. envoy Dennis Ross returned from a trip to the region set to begin at the end of this week.
